n: This chapter is one long “if…then” sentence in Hebrew. The “if” begins here: if you take my words to heart and treasure my commands like something valuable you store away.
Seeking wisdom involves both listening (the ear) and caring deeply (the heart). In Hebrew thought the heart is the center of thinking and choosing, not only feeling.
Wisdom must be wanted. The seeker cries out for understanding like someone calling desperately for help.
Search for wisdom the way miners dig for silver or treasure hunters search for buried gold—with effort and persistence.
The “then” arrives: if you seek wisdom like that, you will come to understand reverence for the Lord and actually come to know God.
Wisdom is ultimately a gift. Human effort seeks it, but the Lord gives it. Both sides matter.
The Lord stores up wisdom for the upright and is their shield.
God watches over the paths of justice and protects the way of his faithful ones.
Another “then”: the seeker will understand what is right, just, and fair—every good road in life.
The key moment is when wisdom moves from outside instruction to inner delight—when it enters your heart and you enjoy it.

f.w: knowledge is pleasant unto thy soul

n: Good judgment becomes a bodyguard, watching over you from within.
Wisdom’s first rescue is from evil men and their twisted talk.

f.g: froward = perverse, twisted, contrary to what is right.

n: These men deliberately leave straight paths to walk in darkness. The image of two paths—light and dark—runs through Proverbs.

f.w: walk in the ways of darkness

n: Worse than doing evil is delighting in it—enjoying the perverse ways of the wicked.
Their roads are crooked and their paths devious—the opposite of the straight path of wisdom.
Wisdom’s second rescue is from the “strange woman”—the adulteress—who uses smooth words. This warning returns in chapters 5–7.

f.g: Literally a woman who is a “stranger” to you—another man’s wife or a woman outside the covenant; here an adulteress.

n: She has abandoned the husband of her youth and broken the marriage covenant made before God. Marriage is described as a sacred covenant, not just a contract.

f.g: Her husband, the companion of her youth.

n: Her house slopes downward toward death. Adultery is pictured as a road that leads to spiritual and physical ruin.

f.g: Hebrew rephaim—the shades, the departed spirits of the dead.

n: Those who go to her don’t easily come back to the path of life. The warning shows how hard it is to recover from such a choice.

f.w: None that go unto her return again

n: Wisdom’s goal is positive: to keep you walking with good people on righteous paths.
The upright will live in the land. For Israel, dwelling in the promised land was the sign of covenant blessing.

f.w: the upright shall dwell in the land

n: The contrast: the wicked will be uprooted from the land like a weed. The chapter ends with the two destinies side by side.
